passages.t: Asa seeks the LORD, and the land has rest
passages.happening:
Abijah dies, Asa reigns, and the land has ten years of peace (verse 1). ‘And Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God’ (verse 2). ‘He removed the foreign altars and high places, shattered the sacred pillars, and chopped down the Asherah poles’ (verse 3). He commands Judah to seek the LORD and keep the law (verse 4).

Because the land is at peace, he builds fortified cities, ‘because the LORD had given him rest’ (verse 6). He tells Judah, “The land is still ours because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought Him and He has given us rest on every side” (verse 7). His army is 300,000 from Judah with large shields and spears, and 280,000 from Benjamin with small shields and bows (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Asa receives the longest treatment of any king so far after Solomon, chapters 14 to 16, and his reign is told in two halves: many years of seeking God, then a late turn to self-reliance. He reigned forty-one years, about 911 to 870 BC. This chapter shows the first half at its best: reform leads to rest, rest to building, and a crisis to one of the finest prayers in the book.

His reform targets the marks of Canaanite religion. Foreign altars served other gods. High places were hilltop or local shrines; some were used for the LORD himself, but the law called for sacrifice at the one place God would choose, and the high places easily blended Israel's worship with its neighbors'. Sacred pillars were standing stones for a deity, and Asherah poles were wooden objects for the goddess Asherah, often set beside altars.

Seek, darash, is the Chronicler's master word for true religion and comes three times. Rest, nuach, is a covenant gift, promised when Israel entered the land and given to Solomon. Building walls and store cities was expected of a king; here the building happens because God has given rest, not instead of trusting him. Judah's heavy infantry and Benjamin's archers reflect real divisions of an ancient army.
passages.later: Moses spoke of the day when God would give rest in the land: ‘He gives you rest from all the enemies around you and you dwell securely’ (Deuteronomy 12:10).
passages.asks: Asa built in the time of rest, and he credited the rest to seeking God. Ask what God has given you in a season of quiet, and what you are building with it. And ask whether you would still seek him if the quiet ended.

passages.t: Asa's prayer, and the victory over Zerah
passages.happening:
‘Then Zerah the Cushite came against them with an army of 1,000,000 men and 300 chariots, and they advanced as far as Mareshah’ (verse 9). Asa goes out to meet him and cries out, “O LORD, there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty. Help us, O LORD our God, for we rely on You, and in Your name we have come against this multitude. O LORD, You are our God. Do not let a mere mortal prevail against You” (verse 11).

‘So the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites fled’ (verse 12). Asa pursues them as far as Gerar, and Judah carries off plunder from the towns around Gerar and from the herders' camps (verses 13-15).
passages.hearers:
Kings praises Asa's removal of idols and tells of his war with Baasha of Israel, but Zerah's invasion appears only in Chronicles. Zerah is called a Cushite and has not been identified with certainty outside the Bible. Some suggest he was a commander serving the pharaoh Osorkon the First, Shishak's successor; others think he led Cushite groups settled in the southern border region, since the battle ends near Gerar and the plunder includes tents, sheep and camels, the property of herders rather than a pharaoh's army. The text does not call him a king. Mareshah was one of Rehoboam's fortress towns in the western foothills; Gerar lay to the south-west, where Abraham and Isaac had lived.

The prayer is the center of the chapter. It confesses that no one but God can help the powerless, asks for help, rely, sha'an, states reliance, and appeals to God's own honor. Verse 13 calls the army the LORD's own. The same verb rely will come back in chapter 16, when Asa relies on the king of Aram instead.
passages.later: A psalm says, ‘God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble’ (Psalm 46:1).
passages.hard:
How should a reader take an army of a million, and a war that ends in plundering towns and herders' tents?

The million is one of the largest figures in Chronicles, and readers take it in the same ways as the numbers in chapter 13: as literal, as counting units rather than individuals, since eleph can mean a clan or military unit, or as a conventional way of saying an overwhelming force. The Chronicler's concern is the contrast between human weakness and God's help.

The plundering of the cities around Gerar and the herders' camps is reported without comment, as ordinary ancient warfare, in which an invader's base and supply towns were treated as targets. The text says the terror of the LORD fell on those cities, which suggests they were linked with Zerah's invasion. Readers today rightly feel the weight of such scenes. The Chronicler presents the war as defense against an invader, not as a model for how God's people should treat others, and the rest of Scripture sets the violence of Israel's wars within a larger story that ends in the peace of God's kingdom.
passages.asks: Asa prayed, There is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty. Ask where you feel powerless, and whether you have prayed that prayer there. And ask whom you know who is powerless, and how you might be part of God's help to them.
